talk: Before an investor puts money in, you agree what the club is worth. That's the pre-money valuation, and adding the new money gives the post-money valuation. The investor's share is their money divided by the post-money value.

terms.meaning: What the company is worth just before the new money goes in.
Your money divided by the post-money value.

questions.prompt: An investor puts $2M into the club at an $8M pre-money valuation. What's the post-money valuation?
working: The new money sits in the club's bank, so the club is now worth more.
whyNot: $8M - $2M = $6M takes the money away. New money adds to the value, because it's sitting in the club's bank.
$8M is the value before the money arrives. After, the club also holds the $2M.
$8M x 2 = $16M doubles it. Just add the money: $8M + $2M = $10M.

questions.prompt: What share of the club does the investor now own?
questions.hint: The investor's money divided by the post-money value.
whyNot: $2M / $8M = 25% divides by the pre-money. The investor's share is their money over the post-money value.
80% is what the existing owners keep: 100% - 20% = 80%.
$2M is the money, not the share. Divide it by the post-money: $2M / $10M = 20%.

questions.prompt: You owned 100% before this round, so you keep 80%. Next year a second investor buys 25% of the bigger club. What do you own then?
questions.hint: A new round shrinks every existing slice by the same share.
working: The new round takes 25%, so every existing owner keeps 100% - 25% = 75% of what they had.
whyNot: 80% - 25% = 55% takes the whole 25% off your share. A new round shrinks everyone's slice in proportion: 80% x 75% = 60%.
75% is what all the old owners keep together, not your share of it.
80% was before the second round. New shares mean a smaller slice.

penalty.prompt: An investor puts {inv} into the club at a {pre} pre-money valuation. What share of the club do they own? (As a percentage.)
penalty.hint: Post-money first, then the investor's money divided by it.

traps.why: That divides by the pre-money. Divide by the post-money: {pre + inv|usd}.
That's what the existing owners keep, not the investor's share.

call.title: The first investor
call.prompt: Two investors each offer $3M to build a new family stand, worth about 1,500 more fans a match. The first values the club at $12M pre-money. The second values it at $9M pre-money. Or you can skip the raise and grow slowly.

options.label: Take $3M at a $12M pre-money
options.result: Good call. $12M + $3M = $15M post-money, so you sell $3M / $15M = 20%. The stand adds 1,500 x $18 = $27,000 profit every matchday. You keep 100% - 20% = 80% of a bigger club, which beats 100% of a smaller one.

options.label: Take $3M at a $9M pre-money
options.result: $9M + $3M = $12M post-money, so you sell $3M / $12M = 25% for the same money. Same stand, but 25% - 20% = 5% more of the club given away.

options.label: Skip the raise
options.result: Safe, but the stand would have added 1,500 x $18 = $27,000 every matchday. Growth you can't fund is growth you don't get.

takeaway: Investor's share = their money / post-money. Post-money = pre-money + the money.
